notes.front: What are a storage account’s endpoints?
notes.back: The addresses formed by combining the account’s unique name with each storage service’s endpoint.
notes.explanation: Every object stored in Azure Storage has an address that includes the account name, so the name is part of every endpoint.
notes.example: Like one building’s street address with a separate labelled door for blobs, files, queues and tables.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Storage account overview”, “Storage account endpoints” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A storage account provides a unique namespace in Azure for your data. Every object that you store in Azure Storage has a URL address that includes your unique account name. The combination of the account name and the service endpoint forms the endpoints for your storage account.

notes.front: What does locally redundant storage (LRS) do?
notes.back: It replicates a storage account’s data within a single physical datacentre in the primary region.
notes.explanation: You can’t choose an availability zone for it, although Azure might move or expand LRS accounts across zones for load balancing.
notes.example: Like keeping several copies of a file in different cabinets of the same building.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Locally redundant storage” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Locally redundant storage (LRS) replicates the data within your storage accounts to a single physical datacenter in the primary region of your choice. Although choosing an availability zone isn't supported, Azure might move or expand LRS accounts across zones to improve load balancing.

notes.front: What does zone-redundant storage (ZRS) do?
notes.back: It copies data synchronously across three or more availability zones in the primary region.
notes.explanation: For applications that need high availability, Microsoft recommends ZRS in the primary region plus replication to a secondary region.
notes.example: Like keeping copies in three separate buildings across one city, each with its own power supply.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Redundancy in the primary region” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) copies your data synchronously across three or more Azure availability zones in the primary region. For applications requiring high availability, Microsoft recommends using ZRS in the primary region, and also replicating to a secondary region.

notes.front: What does geo-redundant storage (GRS) do?
notes.back: It copies data with LRS in the primary region, then asynchronously to a secondary region hundreds of miles away.
notes.explanation: Only the copy to the secondary region is asynchronous; the copies in the primary region are made synchronously.
notes.example: Like keeping copies in one office and posting a further copy to a branch in a distant city.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Geo-redundant storage” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Geo-redundant storage (GRS) copies your data synchronously to one or more availability zones in the primary region by using LRS. It then copies your data asynchronously to a secondary region that is hundreds of miles away from the primary region.

notes.front: What does geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) do?
notes.back: It uses ZRS across availability zones in the primary region, then copies data asynchronously to a secondary region.
notes.explanation: Within the secondary region, the data is then copied synchronously with LRS.
notes.example: Like copies in three buildings across one city, plus a posted copy kept in a single building elsewhere.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Redundancy in a secondary region” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) copies your data synchronously across three or more Azure availability zones in the primary region by using ZRS. It then copies your data asynchronously to the secondary region. Within the secondary region, your data is copied synchronously by using LRS.

notes.front: What is object replication in Azure Storage?
notes.back: A feature that asynchronously copies block blobs from a source storage account to a destination account.
notes.explanation: It is used to cut read latency, make compute workloads more efficient, optimise data distribution and reduce costs.
notes.example: Like a courier who periodically carries new documents from head office to a regional office’s filing cabinet.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Object replication for block blobs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Object replication asynchronously copies block blobs between a source storage account and a destination account. Use object replication to minimize latency on read requests, to increase efficiency for compute workloads, to optimize data distribution, and to minimize costs.

notes.front: In object replication, what do the replication policy and its rules specify?
notes.back: The policy names the source and destination accounts; each rule names a source and destination container and which blobs replicate.
notes.explanation: A policy holds one or more rules, so one account pair can cover several container pairs.
notes.example: Like a removals contract naming two houses, with one line per room saying where that room’s boxes go.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Object replication for block blobs”, “Object replication policies and rules” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you configure object replication, you create a replication policy that specifies the source storage account and the destination account. A replication policy includes one or more rules that specify a source and destination container, and indicate which source blobs are replicated.

notes.front: What is Azure Storage encryption?
notes.back: Service-side encryption that automatically encrypts data when Azure Storage persists it to the cloud.
notes.explanation: It protects data and helps an organisation meet its security and compliance commitments.
notes.example: Like a safe-deposit vault that locks every box automatically, whether or not the customer asks.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage encryption for data at rest” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Storage uses service-side encryption (SSE) to automatically encrypt your data when it persists to the cloud. Azure Storage encryption protects your data and helps you meet your organizational security and compliance commitments.

notes.front: What is a customer-managed key for a storage account?
notes.back: Your own key, which Azure Storage uses to protect and control access to the key that encrypts the account’s data.
notes.explanation: Your key sits one level above the data: it guards the key that does the encrypting, which gives you more control over access.
notes.example: Like holding the only key to the box where the bank keeps its vault key.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Customer-managed keys for Azure Storage encryption” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can use your own encryption key to protect the data in your storage account. When you specify a customer-managed key, Azure Storage uses that key to protect and control access to the key that encrypts your data. Customer-managed keys offer greater flexibility to manage access controls.
introduces: customer-managed keys for a storage account
uses: customer-managed keys for a storage account

notes.front: What is infrastructure encryption for a storage account?
notes.back: A second layer of encryption at the infrastructure level, so data is encrypted twice with different algorithms and keys.
notes.explanation: If one of the encryption algorithms or keys is compromised, the other layer still protects the data.
notes.example: Like a letter in a locked envelope inside a separately locked box, each with its own key.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage encryption for data at rest”, “Doubly encrypt data with infrastructure encryption” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you enable infrastructure encryption, your data in a storage account is encrypted twice - once at the service level and once at the infrastructure level - with two different encryption algorithms and two different keys. Double encryption of Azure Storage data protects against a scenario where one of the encryption algorithms or keys is compromised.

notes.front: What is an encryption scope in Azure Storage?
notes.back: A way to encrypt with a key scoped to a container or an individual blob, instead of the whole storage account.
notes.explanation: It lets you draw secure boundaries between different customers’ data held in the same storage account.
notes.example: Like a block of flats where each flat has its own lock instead of one shared front-door key.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage encryption for data at rest”, “About encryption key management” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Encryption scopes enable you to manage encryption with a key that is scoped to a container or an individual blob. You can use encryption scopes to create secure boundaries between data that resides in the same storage account but belongs to different customers.

notes.front: What is anonymous read access to blobs?
notes.back: Optional access that lets requests read containers and blobs without authorisation; it is never permitted by default.
notes.explanation: Unless it is explicitly enabled, every request to a container and its blobs must be authorised.
notes.example: Like a shop-window display that anyone passing can look at without a ticket.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview: Remediating anonymous read access for blob data” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Storage supports optional anonymous read access for containers and blobs. By default, anonymous access to your data is never permitted. Unless you explicitly enable anonymous access, all requests to a container and its blobs must be authorized.

notes.front: Which recommended storage account type supports blobs, file shares, queues and tables together?
notes.back: Standard general-purpose v2.
notes.explanation: Microsoft recommends this standard type for most scenarios that use Azure Storage.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Storage account overview”, “Types of storage accounts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Standard storage account type for blobs, file shares, queues, and tables. Recommended for most scenarios that use Azure Storage.

notes.front: Which premium storage account type is meant for block and append blobs with high transaction rates or small objects?
notes.back: Premium block blobs.
notes.explanation: It is also the recommended type when a workload needs consistently low storage latency.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Storage account overview”, “Types of storage accounts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Premium storage account type for block blobs and append blobs. Recommended for scenarios with high transaction rates or that use smaller objects or require consistently low storage latency.

notes.front: Which storage account type should you choose for one account that holds both Server Message Block and Network File System file shares?
notes.back: Premium file shares.
notes.explanation: It holds file shares only and is recommended for enterprise or high-performance scale applications.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Storage account overview”, “Types of storage accounts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Premium storage account type for file shares only. Recommended for enterprise or high-performance scale applications. Use this account type if you want a storage account that supports both Server Message Block (SMB) and NFS file shares.

notes.front: Which premium storage account type holds nothing but page blobs?
notes.back: Premium page blobs.
notes.explanation: Unlike general-purpose v2, it can’t hold other blob types, files, queues or tables.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Storage account overview”, “Types of storage accounts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Premium storage account type for page blobs only.

notes.front: Can you change a storage account to a different type after it is created?
notes.back: No. You must create a new account of the other type and copy the data into it.
notes.explanation: Moving to another type is therefore a data migration, not a settings change.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Storage account overview”, “Types of storage accounts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can't change a storage account to a different type after it's created. To move your data to a storage account of a different type, you must create a new account and copy the data to the new account.

notes.front: A small web app needs blob storage, a queue and a table, with no special performance needs. Which storage account type fits?
notes.back: Standard general-purpose v2.
notes.choices:
A) Standard general-purpose v2
B) Premium block blobs
C) Premium file shares
D) Premium page blobs
notes.choicesExplained: B holds only block and append blobs. C holds only file shares. D holds only page blobs. None of them can also hold queues and tables.
notes.explanation: Only the standard general-purpose v2 type covers blobs, queues and tables in one account, and it suits most scenarios.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Storage account overview”, “Types of storage accounts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Standard storage account type for blobs, file shares, queues, and tables. Recommended for most scenarios that use Azure Storage.

notes.front: A storage account name must be between {{c1::3 and 24}} characters long.
notes.explanation: The same rule set also limits which characters the name may contain.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Storage account overview”, “Storage account name” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Storage account names must be between 3 and 24 characters in length. They can contain only numbers and lowercase letters.

notes.front: Which characters may a storage account name contain, and how unique must it be?
notes.back: Only numbers and lowercase letters; it must be unique within Azure.
notes.explanation: No two storage accounts anywhere in Azure can share a name.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Storage account overview”, “Storage account name” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: They can contain only numbers and lowercase letters. - Your storage account name must be unique within Azure. No two storage accounts can have the same name.

notes.front: Which of these could be a valid storage account name?
notes.back: payrollarchive26
notes.choices:
A) Payroll-Archive
B) payrollarchive26
C) pa
D) payrolldepartmentarchive2026
notes.choicesExplained: A uses capitals and a hyphen. C has only 2 characters. D has 28 characters, over the limit of 24.
notes.explanation: It uses only lowercase letters and numbers and is within 3 to 24 characters; it must also be free across Azure.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Storage account overview”, “Storage account name” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Storage account names must be between 3 and 24 characters in length. They can contain only numbers and lowercase letters. - Your storage account name must be unique within Azure.

notes.front: When creating a storage account, which performance option does Microsoft recommend for most scenarios?
notes.back: Standard, which creates a general-purpose v2 account (the default).
notes.explanation: Premium is for scenarios that require low latency.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create an Azure storage account”, “Basics tab” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence:
This type of account is recommended by Microsoft for most scenarios. For more information, see Types of storage accounts.

Select **Premium** for scenarios requiring low latency.

notes.front: When you create a storage account with Azure CLI or Azure PowerShell, which parameter sets the account type?
notes.back: `kind`, for example `StorageV2`.
notes.explanation: Performance and redundancy are set together in a separate parameter, `sku` or `SkuName`, such as `Standard_GRS`.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create an Azure storage account”, “Storage account type parameters” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: specify the storage account type by using the `kind` parameter (for example, `StorageV2`). Specify the performance tier and redundancy configuration together by using the `sku` or `SkuName` parameter (for example, `Standard_GRS`).

notes.front: You script a standard general-purpose v2 account that needs zone redundancy, a copy in a secondary region and read access there. Which `sku` value do you pass?
notes.back: `Standard_RAGZRS`, with `kind` set to `StorageV2`.
notes.explanation: Standard general-purpose v2 accepts all six redundancy values, and the read-access geo-zone-redundant one is `Standard_RAGZRS`.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create an Azure storage account”, “Storage account type parameters” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Standard general-purpose v2 | LRS / GRS / RA-GRS / ZRS / GZRS / RA-GZRS | StorageV2 | Standard_LRS / Standard_GRS / Standard_RAGRS/ Standard_ZRS / Standard_GZRS / Standard_RAGZRS

notes.front: While creating a storage account in the portal, you must switch on infrastructure encryption. Which tab do you use?
notes.back: Encryption.
notes.choices:
A) Basics
B) Advanced
C) Encryption
D) Data protection
notes.choicesExplained: A holds the essentials such as name, region, performance and redundancy. B holds options such as the hierarchical namespace. D holds recovery and tracking options for blob data.
notes.explanation: The Enable infrastructure encryption setting sits on the Encryption tab, and it must be chosen while the account is created.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Enable infrastructure encryption for double encryption of data”, “Create an account with infrastructure encryption enabled” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: On the **Encryption** tab, locate **Enable infrastructure encryption**, and select **Enabled**.

notes.front: Which kind of managed identity must you use when you configure customer-managed keys while creating a storage account?
notes.back: A user-assigned managed identity.
notes.explanation: On an existing account, a system-assigned managed identity is also allowed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Customer-managed keys for Azure Storage encryption”, “Customer-managed keys with a key vault in the same tenant” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you configure customer-managed keys at the time that you create a storage account, you must use a user-assigned managed identity. - When you configure customer-managed keys on an existing storage account, you can use either a user-assigned managed identity or a system-assigned managed identity.
uses: customer-managed keys for a storage account

notes.front: Which redundancy option is the lowest-cost and least durable?
notes.back: LRS.
notes.explanation: It still protects data against drive, server and rack failures.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Locally redundant storage” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: LRS is the lowest-cost redundancy option and offers the least durability compared to other options. LRS protects your data against drive, server, and rack failures.

notes.front: A render farm writes intermediate frames that can be regenerated in minutes if lost. Which redundancy option fits at the lowest cost?
notes.back: LRS.
notes.explanation: Microsoft suggests considering LRS when data can easily be reconstructed after a loss, and it is the cheapest option.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Locally redundant storage” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If your application stores data that can be easily reconstructed if data loss occurs, consider choosing LRS.

notes.front: How many nines of yearly object durability do LRS, ZRS, GRS and GZRS offer, at least?
notes.back: LRS 11, ZRS 12, GRS and GZRS 16.
notes.explanation: The two geo-redundant options share the highest figure, and LRS has the lowest.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Durability and availability parameters” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Percent durability of objects over a given year | at least 99.999999999% (11 9s) | at least 99.9999999999% (12 9s) | at least 99.99999999999999% (16 9s) | at least 99.99999999999999% (16 9s) |

notes.front: Does storage redundancy protect you against accidental deletes or overwrites?
notes.back: No. Deletes and overwrites reach every copy at once; redundancy protects against hardware failure.
notes.explanation: Every replica holds the same current state, so a mistaken change is copied to all of them.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Locally redundant storage” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: All replicas reflect the same current state: deletions and overwrites are applied to all copies simultaneously. Redundancy protects against hardware failure, not against data-modifying operations.

notes.front: A manager says, “We use GZRS, so if someone overwrites a blob by mistake we can get the old one from the secondary region.” Is that right?
notes.back: No. The overwrite is applied to all replicas, including the secondary copy.
notes.explanation: Redundancy guards against hardware failure, not against changes to the data, so a separate recovery feature is needed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Locally redundant storage” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: All replicas reflect the same current state: deletions and overwrites are applied to all copies simultaneously. Redundancy protects against hardware failure, not against data-modifying operations.

notes.front: When does a write to a ZRS account return success?
notes.back: Only after the data is written to all replicas across the three availability zones.
notes.explanation: If a zone is temporarily unavailable, success comes once all available zones have the data.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Zone-redundant storage” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A write request to a storage account that's using ZRS happens synchronously. The write operation returns successfully only after the data is written to all replicas across the three availability zones. If an availability zone is temporarily unavailable, the operation returns successfully after the data is written to all available zones.

notes.front: Regulations say a dataset must stay in one Azure region, but the app must stay available if a datacentre fails. Which redundancy option fits?
notes.back: ZRS.
notes.choices:
A) LRS
B) ZRS
C) GRS
D) GZRS
notes.choicesExplained: A keeps every copy in a single datacentre. C and D copy data to a secondary region, which the rule forbids.
notes.explanation: Microsoft recommends ZRS both for high availability and for keeping replication within one region for data governance.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Zone-redundant storage” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Microsoft recommends using ZRS in the primary region for scenarios that require high availability. ZRS is also recommended for restricting replication of data to a particular region to meet data governance requirements.

notes.front: Can you choose which secondary region a geo-redundant account replicates to?
notes.back: No. The paired secondary region is determined by the primary region and can’t be changed.
notes.explanation: At creation you select only the primary region; the pairing follows from it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Redundancy in a secondary region” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you create a storage account, you select the primary region for the account. The paired secondary region is determined based on the primary region, and can't be changed.

notes.front: Why might a failure in the primary region lose data in a GRS account?
notes.back: Replication to the secondary region is asynchronous, so the latest writes may not have arrived there.
notes.explanation: The loss happens only if the primary region can’t be recovered.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Redundancy in a secondary region” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Because data is replicated to the secondary region asynchronously, a failure that affects the primary region might result in data loss if the primary region can't be recovered.

notes.front: A standard account must survive a regional disaster and must also let blobs be moved to the archive tier. Which option fits?
notes.back: GRS.
notes.choices:
A) LRS
B) ZRS
C) GRS
D) GZRS
notes.choicesExplained: A and B keep all data in the primary region. D has a secondary region, but the archive tier isn’t supported for GZRS accounts.
notes.explanation: Archive works with LRS, GRS and read-access GRS accounts, and of those only GRS adds a secondary region.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Supported storage account types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The archive tier for Blob Storage is supported for LRS, GRS, and RA-GRS accounts, but not for ZRS, GZRS, or RA-GZRS accounts.

notes.front: An account must keep accepting reads and writes if an availability zone fails, and must stay durable if the whole primary region is lost. Which option fits?
notes.back: GZRS.
notes.choices:
A) LRS
B) ZRS
C) GRS
D) GZRS
notes.choicesExplained: A keeps all copies in one datacentre. B has no secondary region. C uses LRS in the primary region, so its primary copies aren’t spread across zones.
notes.explanation: GZRS keeps reads and writes going through a zone outage and keeps data durable through a regional outage.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Geo-zone-redundant storage” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: With a GZRS account, you can continue to read and write data if an availability zone becomes unavailable or is unrecoverable. Additionally, your data also remains durable during a complete regional outage or a disaster in which the primary region isn't recoverable.

notes.front: With plain GRS or GZRS, can applications read the secondary region’s data without a failover?
notes.back: No. Reading the secondary needs read-access geo-redundant or read-access geo-zone-redundant storage.
notes.explanation: Without a failover, the secondary copy is neither readable nor writable.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Redundancy in a secondary region” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you use GRS or GZRS, the data in the secondary region isn't available for read or write access unless there's a failover to the secondary region. For read access to the secondary region, configure your storage account to use read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS) or read-access geo-zone-redundant storage (RA-GZRS).

notes.front: A reporting app must keep reading data from the secondary region during a primary-region outage, without waiting for a failover. Which configuration fits?
notes.back: Read-access geo-zone-redundant storage.
notes.choices:
A) GRS
B) GZRS
C) Read-access geo-zone-redundant storage
D) ZRS
notes.choicesExplained: A and B copy data to the secondary region but don’t allow reads there without a failover. D has no secondary region.
notes.explanation: Read access to the secondary during a primary outage is available only with the read-access forms of GRS and GZRS.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Durability and availability by outage scenario” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Read access to the secondary region is available if the primary region becomes unavailable | No | No | Yes (with RA-GRS) | Yes (with RA-GZRS) |

notes.front: What is the main difference between GRS and GZRS?
notes.back: How data is replicated in the primary region: LRS for GRS, ZRS across zones for GZRS.
notes.explanation: In the secondary region both use LRS, so the difference lies entirely in the primary region.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Redundancy in a secondary region” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The primary difference between GRS and GZRS is how data is replicated in the primary region. Within the secondary region, data is always replicated synchronously by using LRS.

notes.front: Can Azure Files use read-access geo-redundant or read-access geo-zone-redundant storage?
notes.back: No, neither.
notes.explanation: For file shares, geo-redundancy gives a secondary copy but no read access to it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage redundancy”, “Read access to data in the secondary region” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Files doesn't support read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS) or read-access geo-zone-redundant storage (RA-GZRS).

notes.front: Which feature must be enabled on the source account, and only there, for object replication?
notes.back: Change feed.
notes.explanation: Blob versioning, by contrast, must be enabled on both the source and destination accounts.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Object replication for block blobs”, “Prerequisites and caveats for object replication” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Change feed: Enable on the source account. To learn how to enable change feed, see Enable and disable the change feed. - Blob versioning: Enable on both the source and destination accounts.

notes.front: Object replication requires blob versioning on {{c1::both the source and destination accounts}}.
notes.explanation: When a replicated blob changes, the source keeps its previous state as a version, and both current and previous versions are replicated.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Object replication for block blobs”, “Blob versioning” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Object replication requires that you enable blob versioning on both the source and destination accounts. When you modify a replicated blob in the source account, the service creates a new version of the blob in the source account that reflects the previous state of the blob, before modification.

notes.front: You try to set up object replication. The source account has change feed and blob versioning on; the destination has neither. What must you add?
notes.back: Blob versioning on the destination account.
notes.explanation: Versioning is needed on both accounts, but change feed only on the source.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Object replication for block blobs”, “Prerequisites and caveats for object replication” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Change feed: Enable on the source account. To learn how to enable change feed, see Enable and disable the change feed. - Blob versioning: Enable on both the source and destination accounts.

notes.front: Which storage account types can take part in object replication?
notes.back: General-purpose v2 and premium block blob accounts, for both source and destination.
notes.explanation: An account of any other type, such as premium page blobs, can’t be a source or a destination.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Object replication for block blobs”, “Prerequisites and caveats for object replication” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Object replication supports general-purpose v2 storage accounts and premium block blob accounts. Both the source and destination accounts must be either general-purpose v2 or premium block blob accounts.

notes.front: Analysts on another continent need fast reads of block blobs held in a general-purpose v2 account. Which feature brings the data closer to them?
notes.back: Object replication.
notes.choices:
A) Object replication
B) GRS
C) ZRS
D) Infrastructure encryption
notes.choicesExplained: B’s secondary copy can’t be read without a failover or read access, and you can’t choose its region. C stays in one region. D is about encryption, not location.
notes.explanation: Object replication lets clients read data from a region physically closer to them, which reduces read latency.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Object replication for block blobs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Object replication reduces latency for read requests by enabling clients to consume data from a region in closer physical proximity.

notes.front: Are the source and destination accounts immediately in sync under object replication?
notes.back: No. Block blob data is replicated asynchronously.
notes.explanation: The copy is made some time after the source write, not as part of it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Object replication for block blobs”, “How object replication works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Because block blob data is replicated asynchronously, the source account and destination account aren't immediately in sync.

notes.front: An app uploads a block blob to the source account and at once reads it from the destination, but it isn’t there yet. Is replication broken?
notes.back: Not necessarily: replication is asynchronous, and its latency depends on the blob’s size.
notes.explanation: Azure Storage checks the source’s change feed periodically and then copies writes asynchronously.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Object replication for block blobs”, “Object replication policies and rules” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: After you configure object replication, Azure Storage checks the change feed for the source account periodically, and asynchronously replicates any write or delete operations to the destination account. Replication latency depends on the size of the block blob being replicated.

notes.front: What happens to object replication when a blob in the source or destination is moved to the archive tier?
notes.back: Replication fails for that blob.
notes.explanation: Bringing the blob back online doesn’t restart replication; only a later update to its data does.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Object replication for block blobs”, “Blob tiering” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: However, object replication fails if a blob in either the source or destination account is moved to the archive tier. Rehydrating an archived blob doesn't trigger object replication. Object replication is triggered only when the blob data is updated again after rehydration.

notes.front: On which account do you first create an object replication policy?
notes.back: The destination account; you then associate it with the source account using its policy identifier.
notes.explanation: Azure Storage gives the policy an identifier when it is created, and that identifier links the two accounts.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Object replication for block blobs”, “Replication policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you configure object replication, you create a replication policy on the destination account through the Azure Storage resource provider. After you create the replication policy, Azure Storage assigns it a policy ID. You must then associate that replication policy with the source account by using the policy ID.

notes.front: A team wants one source account to replicate the same container to three regional accounts. Can one source do this?
notes.back: No. A source account can replicate to at most two destination accounts.
notes.explanation: Each destination needs its own policy, and a source is limited to two.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Object replication for block blobs”, “Replication policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A source account can replicate to no more than two destination accounts, with one policy for each destination account.

notes.front: By default, does a new replication rule copy blobs that already exist in the source container?
notes.back: No. Only block blobs added after the rule is created are copied, unless you choose otherwise.
notes.explanation: You can opt to copy existing blobs too, or set a custom copy scope from a chosen time.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Object replication for block blobs”, “Replication rules” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: After you create a replication rule, preexisting blobs are ignored; only new block blobs added after the rule is created are copied by default. However, you can specify that both new and existing block blobs are copied. You can also define a custom copy scope that copies any block blobs created after a specified time.

notes.front: Can you write to a destination container while a replication policy is in place?
notes.back: No. Writes to the destination container aren’t permitted.
notes.explanation: Attempts fail with error 409 (Conflict); to write there you must first disable replication.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Object replication for block blobs”, “Replication rules” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: After you create the replication policy, write operations to the destination container aren't permitted. Any attempts to write to the destination container fail with error code 409 (Conflict). To write to a destination container with a replication rule, you must first disable replication.

notes.front: Must object replication’s source and destination accounts share a region or subscription?
notes.back: No. They can be in different regions, subscriptions, or even Microsoft Entra tenants.
notes.explanation: Only one replication policy is allowed for each source and destination account pair.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Object replication for block blobs”, “Replication policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The source and destination accounts might be in the same region or in different regions. They might also reside in the same subscription or in different subscriptions. Optionally, the source and destination accounts might reside in different Microsoft Entra tenants. You can create only one replication policy for each source and destination account pair.

notes.front: Azure Storage encryption is enabled for all storage accounts, and you {{c1::can’t disable it}}.
notes.explanation: Because data is secured by default, no code or application changes are needed to benefit from it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage encryption for data at rest”, “About Azure Storage service-side encryption” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Storage encryption is enabled for all storage accounts. You can't disable Azure Storage encryption. Because your data is secured by default, you don't need to modify your code or applications to take advantage of Azure Storage encryption.

notes.front: A developer asks you to turn off Azure Storage encryption on a test account and to change the app so it decrypts data. What do you tell them?
notes.back: Neither is possible or needed: the encryption can’t be disabled and needs no code changes.
notes.explanation: Encryption is on for every storage account by default and is transparent to applications.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage encryption for data at rest”, “About Azure Storage service-side encryption” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Storage encryption is enabled for all storage accounts. You can't disable Azure Storage encryption. Because your data is secured by default, you don't need to modify your code or applications to take advantage of Azure Storage encryption.

notes.front: Does Azure Storage encryption depend on the performance tier or the access tier?
notes.back: No. Data is encrypted in every tier, including blobs in the archive tier.
notes.explanation: All new and existing block, append and page blobs are encrypted.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage encryption for data at rest”, “About Azure Storage service-side encryption” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Data in a storage account is encrypted regardless of performance tier (standard or premium) or access tier (hot or cool). All new and existing block blobs, append blobs, and page blobs are encrypted, including blobs in the archive tier.

notes.front: Which keys encrypt a new storage account’s data by default?
notes.back: Microsoft-managed keys.
notes.explanation: You can keep relying on them or manage encryption with your own keys instead.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage encryption for data at rest”, “About encryption key management” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Data in a new storage account is encrypted with Microsoft-managed keys by default. You can continue to rely on Microsoft-managed keys for the encryption of your data, or you can manage encryption with your own keys.

notes.front: If you have your own key rotation requirements, what does Microsoft recommend over Microsoft-managed keys?
notes.back: Customer-managed keys, so you can manage and audit rotation yourself.
notes.explanation: Microsoft-managed keys are rotated by Microsoft according to compliance requirements, not by you.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage encryption for data at rest”, “About encryption key management” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Microsoft-managed keys are rotated appropriately per compliance requirements. If you have specific key rotation requirements, Microsoft recommends that you move to customer-managed keys so that you can manage and audit the rotation yourself.
uses: customer-managed keys for a storage account

notes.front: An auditor requires your company to set its own key rotation schedule for a storage account and to audit each rotation. Which key option fits?
notes.back: Customer-managed keys.
notes.choices:
A) Microsoft-managed keys
B) Customer-managed keys
C) Infrastructure encryption
D) Anonymous read access settings
notes.choicesExplained: A is rotated by Microsoft, not on your schedule. C adds a second layer that uses Microsoft-managed keys. D controls access, not keys.
notes.explanation: With customer-managed keys, rotation is your responsibility, so you can manage and audit it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage encryption for data at rest”, “About encryption key management” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you have specific key rotation requirements, Microsoft recommends that you move to customer-managed keys so that you can manage and audit the rotation yourself.
uses: customer-managed keys for a storage account

notes.front: Which two Azure key stores can hold customer-managed keys for a storage account?
notes.back: Azure Key Vault and Azure Key Vault Managed Hardware Security Module.
notes.explanation: You can create the keys yourself and store them there, or generate them with the Key Vault interfaces.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Customer-managed keys for Azure Storage encryption” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You must use one of the following Azure key stores to store your customer-managed keys: - Azure Key Vault - Azure Key Vault Managed Hardware Security Module (HSM) You can either create your own keys and store them in the key vault or managed HSM, or you can use the Azure Key Vault APIs to generate keys.
uses: customer-managed keys for a storage account

notes.front: Which two protections must be enabled on the key vault that holds a storage account’s customer-managed key?
notes.back: Soft delete and purge protection.
notes.explanation: The key itself must also be of a supported type and size: 2048, 3072 or 4096 bits.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Customer-managed keys for Azure Storage encryption”, “Key vault requirements” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The key vault or managed HSM that stores the key must meet the following requirements: - Soft delete is enabled. - Purge protection is enabled. - The key is an RSA or RSA-HSM key. - The key size is 2048, 3072, or 4096.
uses: customer-managed keys for a storage account

notes.front: You try to use a key from an existing key vault as a storage account’s customer-managed key. The vault has soft delete on but purge protection off. What must change?
notes.back: Enable purge protection on the key vault.
notes.explanation: A vault holding a customer-managed key needs both soft delete and purge protection enabled.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Customer-managed keys for Azure Storage encryption”, “Key vault requirements” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The key vault or managed HSM that stores the key must meet the following requirements: - Soft delete is enabled. - Purge protection is enabled.
uses: customer-managed keys for a storage account

notes.front: You rotate a customer-managed key that a storage account picks up automatically. How long should you wait before disabling the old key version?
notes.back: 24 hours.
notes.explanation: Azure Storage checks the key vault for a new key version only once a day.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Customer-managed keys for Azure Storage encryption”, “Automatically update the key version” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Storage checks the key vault for a new key version only once daily. When you rotate a key, wait 24 hours before disabling the older version.
uses: customer-managed keys for a storage account

notes.front: Infrastructure encryption {{c1::can’t be enabled or disabled}} after the storage account has been created.
notes.explanation: It has to be configured at the time the account is created.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Enable infrastructure encryption for double encryption of data”, “Create an account with infrastructure encryption enabled” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To enable infrastructure encryption for a storage account, you must configure a storage account to use infrastructure encryption at the time that you create the account. Infrastructure encryption cannot be enabled or disabled after the account has been created.

notes.front: A compliance rule now demands double encryption for new blob data in an existing account created without infrastructure encryption. Which option works inside that account?
notes.back: Create an encryption scope with infrastructure encryption enabled and use it.
notes.choices:
A) Turn on infrastructure encryption on the account’s Encryption page
B) Create an encryption scope with infrastructure encryption enabled and use it
C) Switch the account to customer-managed keys
D) Nothing: Azure Storage encryption already encrypts twice
notes.choicesExplained: A is impossible: the account-level setting can’t change after creation. C changes who manages the service-level key but adds no second layer. D is wrong: standard encryption is a single, service-level layer.
notes.explanation: When the account lacks infrastructure encryption, you can still enable it for a scope at the time you create that scope.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Enable infrastructure encryption for double encryption of data”, “Create an encryption scope with infrastructure encryption enabled” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If infrastructure encryption is not enabled at the account level, then you have the option to enable it for an encryption scope at the time that you create the scope. The infrastructure encryption setting for an encryption scope cannot be changed after the scope is created.
uses: customer-managed keys for a storage account

notes.front: Which keys does the infrastructure-level layer of double encryption use?
notes.back: Microsoft-managed keys, always a separate key.
notes.explanation: The service-level layer can use customer-managed keys, but the infrastructure layer can’t.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Storage encryption for data at rest”, “Doubly encrypt data with infrastructure encryption” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Service-level encryption supports the use of either Microsoft-managed keys or customer-managed keys with Azure Key Vault. Infrastructure-level encryption relies on Microsoft-managed keys and always uses a separate key.
uses: customer-managed keys for a storage account

notes.front: When is infrastructure encryption recommended?
notes.back: When doubly encrypting data is necessary for compliance requirements.
notes.explanation: For most other scenarios there is unlikely to be a benefit, because Azure Storage encryption is strong enough.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Enable infrastructure encryption for double encryption of data” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Infrastructure encryption is recommended for scenarios where doubly encrypting data is necessary for compliance requirements. For most other scenarios, Azure Storage encryption provides a sufficiently powerful encryption algorithm, and there is unlikely to be a benefit to using infrastructure encryption.

notes.front: If infrastructure encryption is enabled for an account, what about the encryption scopes created in it?
notes.back: They automatically use infrastructure encryption.
notes.explanation: Without it at account level, you can still turn it on for a scope when you create the scope.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Enable infrastructure encryption for double encryption of data”, “Create an encryption scope with infrastructure encryption enabled” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If infrastructure encryption is enabled for an account, then any encryption scope created on that account automatically uses infrastructure encryption. If infrastructure encryption is not enabled at the account level, then you have the option to enable it for an encryption scope at the time that you create the scope.

notes.front: What are the two broad ways Storage Explorer connects to Azure resources?
notes.back: Signing in to Azure to reach your subscriptions, and attaching to an individual storage resource.
notes.explanation: Signing in reaches the resources in your subscriptions; attaching reaches one resource at a time.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Get started with Storage Explorer”, “Connect to a storage account or service” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Storage Explorer provides several ways to connect to Azure resources: * Sign in to Azure to access your subscriptions and their resources * Attach to an individual Azure Storage resource

notes.front: After you sign in, which permissions does Storage Explorer need to reach storage resources fully?
notes.back: Both management (Azure Resource Manager) and data layer permissions.
notes.explanation: You need permissions for the account, its containers and the data in them.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Get started with Storage Explorer”, “Sign in to Azure” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To fully access resources after you sign in, Storage Explorer requires both management (Azure Resource Manager) and data layer permissions. This means that you need Microsoft Entra permissions to access your storage account, the containers in the account, and the data in the containers.

notes.front: A user has data-layer access to one blob container but no management-layer access. How should they connect in Storage Explorer?
notes.back: Attach to the container and sign in using Microsoft Entra ID.
notes.explanation: Microsoft Entra ID is the preferred attach method when a user has data access but no management access.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Get started with Storage Explorer”, “Microsoft Entra ID” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Microsoft Entra ID is the preferred option if you have data layer access to your resource but no management layer access.

notes.front: Which resources can Storage Explorer attach to with a shared access signature address for the resource?
notes.back: Individual resources: a blob container, a Data Lake Storage container or directory, a file share, a queue or a table.
notes.explanation: A SAS address reaches one resource inside an account; to attach a whole storage account with a shared access signature, you use a SAS connection string instead.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Get started with Storage Explorer”, “Shared access signature (SAS) URL” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Storage Explorer can connect to the following resource types using a SAS URI: * Blob container * Azure Data Lake Storage container or directory * File share * Queue * Table

notes.front: A developer points Storage Explorer at the Azurite emulator on the right ports, but nothing answers. What should they check first?
notes.back: That Azurite is actually running: Storage Explorer doesn’t start emulators.
notes.explanation: The emulator must be started manually before Storage Explorer can connect to it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Get started with Storage Explorer”, “Local storage emulator” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Storage Explorer doesn't automatically start your emulator. You must start it manually.

notes.front: How do you start generating an account-level shared access signature in Storage Explorer?
notes.back: Right-click the storage account and select Get Shared Access Signature.
notes.explanation: It starts from the storage account’s own context menu in the explorer tree.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Get started with Storage Explorer”, “Account level shared access signature” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Right-click the storage account you want share, and then select **Get Shared Access Signature**.

notes.front: As the Owner of a storage account, you {{c1::aren’t automatically assigned}} permissions to access its data.
notes.explanation: So before AzCopy can do anything useful, you must decide how to provide authorisation credentials.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Get started with AzCopy”, “Authorize AzCopy” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: As an owner of your Azure Storage account, you aren't automatically assigned permissions to access data. Before you can do anything meaningful with AzCopy, you need to decide how you'll provide authorization credentials to the storage service.

notes.front: An administrator who holds the Owner role on a storage account signs in and runs an AzCopy upload, which is refused. Why, and what are the two ways forward?
notes.back: Owner doesn’t grant data access. Authorise with Microsoft Entra ID (with data permissions) or with a shared access signature token.
notes.explanation: Management rights over the account don’t include rights to its data.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Get started with AzCopy”, “Authorize AzCopy” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: As an owner of your Azure Storage account, you aren't automatically assigned permissions to access data. Before you can do anything meaningful with AzCopy, you need to decide how you'll provide authorization credentials to the storage service. You can provide credentials by using Microsoft Entra ID or by using a SAS token.

notes.front: How does authorising AzCopy with Microsoft Entra ID differ from using a shared access signature token?
notes.back: With Microsoft Entra ID you give credentials once; a token must be appended to each command.
notes.explanation: Signing in once saves appending a token to every command.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Get started with AzCopy”, “Authorize with Microsoft Entra ID” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By using Microsoft Entra ID, you provide credentials once instead of appending a SAS token to each command.

notes.front: Which three types of security principal can authorise AzCopy through Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: A user identity, a managed identity or a service principal.
notes.explanation: You start by choosing which of these types you want to authorise.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Get started with AzCopy”, “Authorize with Microsoft Entra ID” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | User identity | Authorize access for AzCopy with a user identity | | Managed identity | Authorize access for AzCopy with a managed identity | | Service principal | Authorize access for AzCopy with a service principal |

notes.front: Which AzCopy command creates a container or file share?
notes.back: `azcopy make`.
notes.explanation: Its counterpart for deleting blobs or files is `azcopy remove`.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Get started with AzCopy”, “List of commands” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: |azcopy make|Creates a container or file share.| |azcopy remove|Deletes blobs or files from an Azure storage account.|

notes.front: You want a destination folder in Blob Storage to mirror a local directory on each run. Which AzCopy command fits?
notes.back: `azcopy sync`.
notes.choices:
A) `azcopy copy`
B) `azcopy sync`
C) `azcopy make`
D) `azcopy bench`
notes.choicesExplained: A copies source data to a destination as a one-off. C only creates a container or file share. D runs a performance benchmark.
notes.explanation: `azcopy sync` replicates the source location to the destination location.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Get started with AzCopy”, “List of commands” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: |azcopy sync|Replicates the source location to the destination location.|

notes.front: Each night, new export files must be pushed to a blob container with nobody at a keyboard. Can AzCopy do this?
notes.back: Yes. Build AzCopy into an automated script as a scheduled data transfer.
notes.explanation: AzCopy runs interactively, but it can also be built into scripts for batch operations, scheduled transfers or continuous integration pipelines.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Get started with AzCopy”, “Transfer data” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can run AzCopy commands interactively. You can also incorporate AzCopy into automated scripts for batch operations, scheduled data transfers, or continuous integration pipelines.

notes.front: Which account property, set to False, makes every blob request to the account require authorisation?
notes.back: `AllowBlobPublicAccess`.
notes.explanation: It overrides each container’s own anonymous access setting.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview: Remediating anonymous read access for blob data”, “Recommendations for remediating anonymous access” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can remediate anonymous access for an account at any time by setting the account's **AllowBlobPublicAccess** property to **False**. After you set the **AllowBlobPublicAccess** property to **False**, all requests for blob data to that storage account will require authorization, regardless of the anonymous access setting for any individual container.

notes.front: A few containers of public product images must stay anonymously readable, but everything else must be locked down. What is the recommended layout?
notes.back: Move those containers into separate storage accounts reserved for anonymous access, and disallow it on all other accounts.
notes.explanation: Keeping anonymous data apart lets you switch anonymous access off everywhere else.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview: Remediating anonymous read access for blob data”, “Scenarios requiring anonymous access” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If your scenario requires that certain containers need to be available for anonymous access, then you should move those containers and their blobs into separate storage accounts that are reserved only for anonymous access. You can then disallow anonymous access for any other storage accounts
